passages.happening:
“In the third month, on the same day of the month that the Israelites had left the land of Egypt, they came to the Wilderness of Sinai” (verse 1).

“After they had set out from Rephidim, they entered the Wilderness of Sinai, and Israel camped there in front of the mountain” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
Everything since the burning bush has been heading here. At the bush God gave Moses a sign: ‘all of you will worship God on this mountain’ (3:12). Now they have arrived. The promised sign has come true.

Israel will stay at this mountain a long time, from here to Numbers 10, nearly a year. All the law of the rest of Exodus, of Leviticus, and of Numbers 1 to 10 is given in this camp.

Where was Mount Sinai? It has not been found by archaeology. Christian tradition since at least the fourth century has placed it at Jebel Musa, Arabic for the mountain of Moses, in the granite peaks of the south of the Sinai Peninsula, where the Monastery of Saint Catherine was built in the sixth century. Others propose nearby Jebel Serbal, peaks in the north of the peninsula nearer Kadesh, or sites in northwest Arabia, the land of Midian. The Old Testament shows little interest in the mountain as a place to visit. The only later figure it sends there is Elijah. These notes take no side on where it was.

Later Jewish tradition linked the giving of the law with the Feast of Weeks, Shavuot, fifty days after Passover. That feast came to celebrate the gift of the Torah as well as the wheat harvest.
passages.later:
Elijah flees to this mountain centuries later: “strengthened by that food, he walked forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God” (1 Kings 19:8).

Paul mentions “Mount Sinai in Arabia” (Galatians 4:25). The phrase is cited in the debate over the mountain's place, though the name Arabia was used loosely in his day.
passages.asks: God brought his people exactly where he said he would. Ask what promise of God you are still waiting to see kept. And ask whether you can trust that the road, however long, leads where he said.

passages.happening:
“Then Moses went up to God, and the LORD called to him from the mountain” (verse 3).

“You have seen for yourselves what I did to Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself” (verse 4).

“Now if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations” (verse 5). “And unto Me you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
These verses are a short poem inside the story, and they are the heart of the covenant. Notice the order. First, what God has done: ‘I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to Myself’. Then what he asks: obey my voice and keep my covenant. Then what he promises: you will be my treasured possession, a kingdom of priests, a holy nation.

Rescue comes first. God does not say: obey me, and I will rescue you. He says: I have rescued you, now be my people. The law that follows is given to people already set free.

‘Brought you to Myself.’ The goal of the exodus was never only freedom from Egypt. It was nearness to God.

‘Treasured possession’ is a word used for a king's own private treasure. Of all the nations, Israel is God's treasure. And yet the very next words are ‘for the whole earth is Mine’. Israel is chosen out of the nations, but for the sake of a whole world that belongs to God.

‘A kingdom of priests.’ A priest stood between God and people, taught God's ways, and brought offerings. Israel as a whole is to stand in that place toward the nations: a people who would show the world what God is like.
passages.later:
Moses later sings of the same care: “As an eagle stirs up its nest and hovers over its young, He spread His wings to catch them and carried them on His pinions” (Deuteronomy 32:11).

Peter gives these words to believers in Christ: “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession” (1 Peter 2:9). Revelation says Christ has made his people “a kingdom and priests to serve our God” (Revelation 5:10). Peter does not take these words away from Israel. Paul, writing of his own people, says, “For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).
passages.asks: God carried his people on eagles' wings and brought them to himself. Ask what it means to you that rescue comes before command. And ask what it would look like for your life to show others what God is like, as a priest would.

passages.happening:
Moses calls the elders and sets before them God's words. “And all the people answered together, ‘We will do everything that the LORD has spoken.’ So Moses brought their words back to the LORD” (verse 8).

“The LORD said to Moses, ‘Behold, I will come to you in a dense cloud, so that the people will hear when I speak with you, and they will always put their trust in you’” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The people answer together, and their answer is wholehearted: ‘We will do everything’. They mean it. The reader who knows the golden calf of chapter 32 may wince, but the promise is real, and it is the right answer.

Moses goes up and down the mountain again and again, carrying words between God and the people. Before any law is given, his place as the go-between is set.

God will come in a thick cloud. The people will hear, but they will not see God. Nothing in this chapter says what God looks like.
passages.later:
The same promise is made again when the covenant is sealed: “All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do” (Exodus 24:3).

Deuteronomy draws the lesson of the cloud: “You heard the sound of the words, but saw no form; there was only a voice” (Deuteronomy 4:12).
passages.asks: The people said, ‘We will do everything’, and meant it. Ask what promises you have made to God with a full heart. And ask what it would take to keep them when the excitement fades.

passages.happening:
God tells Moses, “Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow. They must wash their clothes and be prepared by the third day, for on the third day the LORD will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people” (verses 10-11).

A boundary is to be set around the mountain: “Be careful not to go up on the mountain or touch its base. Whoever touches the mountain shall surely be put to death” (verse 12). “Only when the ram’s horn sounds a long blast may they approach the mountain” (verse 13).

“Be prepared for the third day,” Moses tells the people. “Do not draw near to a woman” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Coming near a god in the ancient world needed preparation. Israel's is simple: wash your clothes, stay behind the boundary, and for three days a husband and wife are not to sleep together.

That last instruction does not treat marriage as sinful. In Israel's law, sexual relations left a couple ritually unclean until evening (Leviticus 15:18), not ready for a time to come near the holy, much as touching a dead body did. Holiness in Israel was not only about right and wrong. It also kept life and death apart in the presence of the living God.

The ram's horn, the shofar, was Israel's trumpet, blown to gather the people, to raise an alarm, or to announce a king.
passages.later:
The same custom appears when David's men may eat the holy bread only because they have kept themselves from women (1 Samuel 21:4-5).

Hebrews remembers how fearful the boundary was: “For they could not bear what was commanded: ‘If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned’” (Hebrews 12:20).
passages.hard:
Why is God so dangerous to approach that even an animal touching the mountain must die? The warnings are severe, and modern readers can find them harsh or arbitrary.

The text's own logic is that holiness is real, and dangerous to whatever is not holy, the way fire is dangerous without being cruel. The rule covers animals because the danger lies in contact, not in guilt. On this reading the boundary is a mercy. God comes near, and he tells the people exactly how to survive his nearness.

Some readers stress that the rules taught reverence at the moment the relationship began; later stories show that God's presence cannot be handled carelessly (Leviticus 10; 2 Samuel 6). Others read the scene as a picture of the distance sin creates, which the rest of Scripture sets out to close.

Both readings agree that the barrier is not the last word. In 24:9-11 Israel's elders go up the mountain, see the God of Israel, and eat and drink in his presence.
passages.asks: God gave the people three days to get ready to meet him. Ask how you prepare yourself to come before God, in worship or in prayer. And ask whether you have treated his presence lightly, or have been too afraid to come near at all.

passages.happening:
“On the third day, when morning came, there was thunder and lightning. A thick cloud was upon the mountain, and a very loud blast of the ram’s horn went out, so that all the people in the camp trembled” (verse 16).

Moses brings the people out to meet God at the foot of the mountain (verse 17). “Mount Sinai was completely enveloped in smoke, because the LORD had descended on it in fire. And the smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked violently” (verse 18).

“And as the sound of the ram’s horn grew louder and louder, Moses spoke and God answered him in the thunder” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
This is a theophany, a visible coming of God. It gathers every sign of power an ancient reader knew: thunder, lightning, thick cloud, fire, smoke like a furnace, earthquake, and a horn growing louder and louder.

The fire in the bush in chapter 3 has become a mountain on fire. The God who spoke to one man from a thornbush now comes down before a whole nation.

Some scholars who place Sinai in northwest Arabia have pointed to volcanic peaks there that might fit the fire and smoke of verse 18. Others see the scene as a great storm. The text's interest is not in the cause but in the one who comes: ‘the LORD had descended on it in fire’.
passages.later:
Hebrews looks back on this day: “For you have not come to a mountain that can be touched and that is burning with fire; to darkness, gloom, and storm; to a trumpet blast or to a voice that made its hearers beg that no further word be spoken” (Hebrews 12:18-19). Instead, believers have come “to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant” (Hebrews 12:24). The contrast does not make God less holy. It says the way to him is now opened through Christ.

At Pentecost, the feast later linked with Sinai, the Spirit came with “a sound like a mighty rushing wind” and “tongues like flames of fire” (Acts 2:2-3). Many readers notice the echo, though Luke does not draw it himself.
passages.asks: The whole mountain shook when God came down. Ask whether your picture of God has room for this kind of holiness and power. And ask what it means to you that this same God invites you near.

passages.happening:
“The LORD descended to the top of Mount Sinai and called Moses to the summit. So Moses went up” (verse 20).

God says, “Go down and warn the people not to break through to see the LORD, lest many of them perish. Even the priests who approach the LORD must consecrate themselves, or the LORD will break out against them” (verses 21-22).

Moses answers that the people cannot come up, since God has already told them to keep the boundary (verse 23). God tells him to go down and bring Aaron, “But the priests and the people must not break through to come up to the LORD, or He will break out against them” (verse 24). “So Moses went down to the people and spoke to them” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
God warns a second time. The danger is real, and God cares enough to warn twice.

‘Break through’ and ‘break out’ are the same Hebrew word. If the people break through the boundary, God's holiness will break out against them. The boundary protects them.

The chapter ends with Moses going down to the people. The next words they will hear are God's own: the Ten Commandments.
passages.later:
Leviticus tells of Aaron's sons who came near carelessly with fire God had not commanded (Leviticus 10:1-2). The warning of Sinai was not empty.

Hebrews ends its comparison of the two mountains with a call to reverence: “let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe” (Hebrews 12:28), for “our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29).
passages.asks: God warned the people twice, because he did not want them to perish. Ask whether you have heard God's warnings as care, or only as restriction. And ask what it would mean to worship him with both thankfulness and awe.
